passage: Okay, so I practised it in the mirror twice, which is embarrassing, but I am telling you because it worked. Devika and I had been together five months, and I kept assuming she would just know what I wanted, and I never asked what she wanted. One evening at the tea stall near her college I said, "Can we talk about what each of us expects? Like how fast we go, how often we meet, when we tell our families." My ears were red. She laughed, then said she wanted to go slower than I did and was not ready to tell her parents yet. I felt a small drop inside. But I said, "Okay. Thank you for saying it. Slower is fine." Honestly it felt better than guessing. We are still working it out. Wasim, signing off!

qa.q: How long had Wasim and Devika been together?
qa.a: They had been together five months.

qa.q: What did Wasim feel when Devika said she wanted to go slower?
qa.a: Wasim felt a small drop inside, a bit of disappointment, but accepted it and thanked her. Talking felt better to Wasim than guessing.

qa.q: What could Wasim and Devika do to keep the conversation going?
qa.a: They could check in now and then and tell each other honestly as feelings change, without expecting mind-reading. 🙂

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when Wasim raised it?
qa.a: She laughed and then answered openly, which suggests relief at being asked rather than assumed. It let her say what she was not ready for.

grounding: The protagonist talks plainly and respectfully with a partner about expectations and accepts a difference.

passage:
Dear Kunal,
I've tried to say this over coffee twice and ended up talking about the weather, so here it is on paper. It feels less embarrassing this way.
We've been together three months, and I realise I've been hoping you'd just guess what I want. That's not fair to either of us.
So: I want us to be exclusive. I like holding hands in public, but I'm not comfortable kissing in front of friends. And about going further physically, I want to go slowly, and I want us to talk about it, not drift into it.
I'd really like to hear what you want too, even if it's different. Different doesn't scare me. Silence does.
Can we talk on Saturday, at the lake, no phones? You can laugh at how formal this letter is. I'm laughing a bit too.
Ganga

qa.q: How long have Ganga and Kunal been together?
Why did Ganga choose to write instead of talking over coffee?
qa.a: Ganga felt too embarrassed to say it aloud, having twice ended up talking about the weather instead.

qa.q: What makes Ganga's letter a respectful way to discuss expectations?
qa.a: It says plainly what Ganga wants and doesn't want, invites Kunal's view even if it differs, and proposes a calm talk at the lake.

qa.q: What would change if Ganga had kept hoping Kunal would guess?
qa.a: Kunal might misread signals, and both could end up hurt or uncomfortable without knowing why.

grounding: Shows discussing what each partner wants plainly and respectfully instead of expecting them to read your mind.

passage:
Lakshmi, you asked how Arvind and I stopped fighting every weekend. Honestly? I stopped expecting him to read my mind.
For months I'd sulk when he booked a movie instead of a quiet dinner, or when he held my hand at my cousin's wedding while I didn't want the whole family watching. I thought, if he really knew me, he'd know.
Then one night, at the dhaba near the highway, I just said it: "Can we each say what we want, even the embarrassing stuff?" My face was burning. I told him I want slow, private affection, and a clear talk before we go further. He said he wants us to be more open in public and to start planning a future together. We don't want the same things on everything.
But now we know. We agreed on some, and we're still talking about the rest.
So that's me, Sangeeta, queen of silent sulking, reformed. Mostly.

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta start the honest talk?
qa.a: At the dhaba near the highway.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when asking "Can we each say what we want"?
qa.a: Embarrassed, with a burning face, but hopeful and determined to stop the silent sulking.

qa.q: What went wrong before, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Sangeeta expected Arvind to guess and sulked when he didn't; saying plainly what each wanted let them agree on some things and keep talking about the rest.

qa.q: How might Arvind see the conversation at the dhaba?
qa.a: As a relief: he finally learns what Sangeeta wants and can share his own wishes openly.

grounding: Illustrates talking about expectations in a relationship without embarrassment, accepting differences instead of expecting mind-reading.
